description: Spacecraft monitor their systems. Astronauts need clear ways to monitor themselves. JAVA SPACE built JAVA VIGIL, a web application that pairs a three-minute reaction-time test with sleep and workload records. Informed by NASA research, it compares attention measurements with personal reference sessions, helping astronauts recognize changes in their performance as they take greater responsibility for their health far from Earth.
summary:
JAVA VIGIL is an interactive crew self-monitoring console designed to help astronauts recognize changes in sustained attention during long-duration space missions. Informed by NASA Human Research Program resources and ISS Psychomotor Vigilance Test research, our working web prototype combines a three-minute reaction-time task with self-reported sleep, sleepiness, schedule, and workload.

Users complete a guided check-in, practice, measurement, and performance review. The console displays response speed, attention lapses, false starts, a response timeline, and measurement-quality information. After three eligible reference sessions, users can compare results with their own personal reference under matching conditions. Records remain in the browser, with optional export for voluntary sharing.

JAVA VIGIL addresses the challenge by helping crew members gather performance indicators, evaluate changes, and identify next steps through established fatigue-reporting procedures. As missions place greater responsibility on astronauts to monitor themselves, this workflow provides concrete observations for informed health discussions. The prototype demonstrates the complete user journey; operational use would require timing calibration, validation, and integration with approved crew procedures.
details:
JAVA VIGIL is a browser-based crew self-monitoring application for sustained attention. It pairs a short reaction-time task with self-reported sleep, schedule, sleepiness, and workload context. The design responds to the health-monitoring challenge by helping crew members gather indicators, review their own results, and identify an appropriate next step.

What the crew can review

The debrief reports mean response speed, median reaction time, lapses at or above 355 ms, and false starts below 130 ms. A response timeline shows when responses slowed or lapsed. Session-quality information flags interruptions that make a result unsuitable for comparison. The application presents task measurements and user-reported context as observations, not diagnoses.

How the measurement is calculated

During the three-minute task, a counter appears after a random 1–4 second interval. The user presses the selected control as soon as it appears. The mean response-speed metric averages 1,000 divided by each valid response time in milliseconds, producing responses per second. Median response time excludes false starts. A response under 130 ms is marked as a false start; a response of 355 ms or longer is counted as a lapse. The Science & Sources panel describes the task rules, including the 30-second response timeout. These thresholds describe task events; they are not medical cutoffs.

When a session can be compared

The application treats comparable conditions as part of the result. Leaving the tab or window, resizing the view, or ending the task early can interrupt or invalidate a session. The quality panel reports logged interruptions and rendering gaps. Browser, display, and input delays can still affect timing, so a clean session means only that the application logged no quality interruption. It does not prove laboratory-grade timing accuracy.

JAVA VIGIL setup and session debrief. Demonstration values are not astronaut data.

Personal reference and records

Reference comparisons become available after three eligible prior sessions marked as reference candidates. The application compares the current session with the median response speed from the latest three comparable references. The same crew alias, self-labeled device, response input, and protocol version are required. Records remain in the browser unless the user chooses to export them as JSON.

This approach lets a user review change against their own repeated records without inventing a population norm. The reference label is self-selected, and device identity is self-reported. If too few eligible reference sessions exist, JAVA VIGIL says so and asks the user to continue building a reference instead of producing a comparison.

Research Basis and Intended Use

NASA’s Human Research Roadmap documents the Psychomotor Vigilance Test on the International Space Station and describes research aims that examine fatigue associated with sleep loss, circadian disruption, and work intensity. NASA Human Research Program resources also describe isolation and confinement, irregular schedules, and workload as factors that can affect crew performance. JAVA VIGIL uses these publications to select contextual check-in fields and to explain why the attention task belongs in a crew health-monitoring workflow.

The application does not ingest NASA datasets or astronaut records. NASA resources inform the design and interpretation; session metrics are generated from the user’s own interaction with the prototype. The Science & Sources panel links the references from inside the app and explains how each informed a feature.

NASA Human Research Roadmap PVT task record and JAVA VIGIL Science & Sources view.

Benefits and intended impact

Long-duration missions place more responsibility on crew members to notice and report changes in their health and performance. JAVA VIGIL gives a crew member a repeatable place to record the conditions around a short attention check and to review the result with its quality information. A personal reference can make gradual change easier to notice, while the sleep and workload record gives the user context for discussing an unexpected result. The intended next step is a better informed review through established crew fatigue-reporting and medical procedures, not an automated treatment or fitness-for-duty decision.

What is distinctive about the prototype

PVT research and spaceflight reaction tests already exist. JAVA VIGIL’s contribution is a browser-based, crew-facing workflow that connects a brief attention task to a contextual check-in, a transparent debrief, personal reference rules, and user-controlled local records. It makes the steps and limitations visible so a user can understand what was measured, when a session can be compared, and what to review next.

Technology and design

JAVA VIGIL is an interactive web prototype built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It supports keyboard or touch input and guides users through check-in, practice, attention measurement, and performance review. For this submission, the public demonstration site is hosted on Netlify. Session records remain in the user’s browser unless voluntarily exported as a JSON file. The prototype is not deployed for astronaut use, connected to NASA systems, or configured to transmit data to mission control.

A future operational version could be adapted for approved onboard hardware and secure reporting workflows, enabling crew members to share results with authorized medical or mission-support personnel. Such integration would require timing calibration, human-factors testing, privacy and security review, and validation against established crew procedures before operational use.

Design factors

The team considered repeatability, input familiarity, interrupted sessions, uncertainty in browser timing, privacy, and interpretability. Practice responses stay outside the measurement history. Reference comparisons require consistent self-labeled conditions. Unknown check-in values remain unknown rather than being filled with estimates. The interface avoids population rankings and makes clear that a browser result cannot replace approved crew procedures.

Validation status

JAVA VIGIL is a functional prototype, not a validated flight instrument. Browser scheduling, display refresh, keyboard or touch latency, and device differences have not been calibrated for flight use. The prototype has not undergone clinical validation. Before operational use, the team would compare timing and scoring with a validated PVT system, test the workflow in a relevant analog environment, and review privacy, human-factors, and crew-procedure requirements. Results do not establish medical diagnoses or fitness for duty.
